title: BrightAI raises $97M to put AI sensors and robots on pipes and power lines
excerpt: BrightAI, which uses AI sensors, robots and drones to watch power lines and pipes, has raised $97M led by Smith Point Capital. GE Vernova also invested.
content_html:
BrightAI has raised $97M led by Smith Point Capital, with customer GE Vernova also investing, bringing its total to $184M. The startup sells AI sensors, inspection robots and a technician assistant that monitor energy, water and industrial sites, and plans to expand into Europe and Asia.

BrightAI, a California startup that uses AI sensors, robots and drones to watch over power lines, pipes and other infrastructure, has raised $97M, it announced on Wednesday. Smith Point Capital, the firm run by former Salesforce co-CEO Keith Block, led the round. Energy company GE Vernova, already a customer, also invested.

The round brings BrightAI’s total funding to $184M. It follows a $51M Series A led by Khosla Ventures and Inspired Capital in July 2025.

BrightAI’s sensors attach to poles, pipelines, compressors and tanks, and run AI on the device to flag problems without a constant internet link. Its robots and drones inspect places too remote or risky for crews. A wearable AI assistant guides technicians through repairs.

The pitch is to fix things before they break. More than half of scheduled inspections find nothing wrong, while serious failures often go unseen until they are underway, BrightAI says.

“Our infrastructure is under more strain than it has ever been, and Physical AI has finally become reliable enough to work in the field,” said founder and CEO Alex Hawkinson.

BrightAI says its platform runs at more than 50,000 sites. Customers include GE Vernova, Diamondback Energy and Kodiak Gas Services. Nearly 60% of its target market is outside North America, and it is opening offices in Europe and Asia.

The grid is under pressure. US utilities are waiting years for transformers and turbines as data centres pile on demand, and plan to spend $1.4T on the grid by 2030. Investors are also backing AI for heavy industry, from autonomous mines to bricklaying robots.
